Heat Events and Heat Mortality: California vs. Arizona, 2007–2025

Yunzhi (Wendy) Zhang

1. Introduction

Research questions

  • Q1. Do California and Arizona experience similar frequencies of heat events?
  • Q2. How different are heat-related deaths between CA and AZ, after accounting for differences in the number of reported heat events?
  • Q3. Are differences in heat-related mortality between CA and AZ driven more by direct or indirect deaths?
  • Q4. Do CA and AZ differ in when heat-related deaths occur and how they have changed over time?

How I arrived at these questions:

During my initial exploration, I noticed that California and Arizona had similar numbers of reported heat events but very different numbers of recorded heat-related deaths. Because they are neighboring states, I wondered whether their geographic proximity would be reflected in similar heat-event patterns and human impacts. The large difference in recorded deaths therefore caught my attention. I developed four related questions to compare heat-event frequency, examine whether the mortality gap persists after accounting for event counts, assess how direct and indirect deaths contribute to the difference, and explore when these deaths occur across seasons and how they have changed over time.

2. Data

Source:

This analysis uses the NOAA Storm Events Database, maintained by the National Centers for Environmental Information (https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/stormevents/). Each record documents a weather event reported by a local National Weather Service office, including its type, location, timing, and the number of direct and indirect deaths, along with a free-text narrative for many events.

Course extract:

I worked with an extract covering 2007–2025 prepared for COMPSS 211B (Data Visualization) at UC Berkeley, provided as two files: event details (storm_events_2007_2025.csv) and event narratives (storm_event_narratives_2007_2025.csv). General cleaning of these files was completed by the course instructor and is not repeated here.

Preparation in this notebook:

I filter the event records to Heat and Excessive Heat events in California and Arizona.

-- Load data
select * from "storm_events_2007_2025.csv";
# Filter the imported data and create year, month, and total deaths.
library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)

heat <- storm_events_2007 |>
  mutate(
    year = year(begin_date_time),
    month = month(begin_date_time, label = TRUE)
  ) |>
  filter(
    state %in% c("CALIFORNIA", "ARIZONA"),
    event_type %in% c("Heat", "Excessive Heat"),
    between(year, 2007, 2025)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    state = str_to_title(state),
    deaths_total = deaths_direct + deaths_indirect
  )
# Check record and episode counts for each state.
heat |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    records = n(),
    episodes = n_distinct(episode_id),
    records_per_episode = records / episodes
  )

Each row in my filtered dataset represents one reported Heat or Excessive Heat event record in California or Arizona, identified by a unique event_id. Multiple records may belong to the same episode, identified by episode_id. Throughout my analysis, “heat events” refers to individual reported records rather than distinct episodes. Total deaths are calculated as direct plus indirect deaths, while the year and month are based on each record’s start date.

3. Analysis

Q1. Do California and Arizona experience similar frequencies of heat events?

I compare annual heat-event counts 2007–2025, then counts by period.

q1_annual <- heat |>
  count(state, year, name = "events") |>
  complete(state, year = 2007:2025, fill = list(events = 0))

ggplot(q1_annual, aes(x = year, y = events, color = state)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Arizona" = "#D55E00",
                                "California" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2007, 2025, 2)) +
  labs(title = "Heat events recorded per year, CA vs AZ",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of event records", color = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

Grouping years into periods to see when the two states’ counts were similar and when they diverged. I split at 2018, when Arizona’s reporting changed.

q1_periods <- heat |>
  mutate(period = case_when(
    year <= 2011 ~ "2007-2011",
    year <= 2017 ~ "2012-2017",
    year <= 2021 ~ "2018-2021",
    TRUE         ~ "2022-2025"
  )) |>
  count(state, period, name = "events")

ggplot(q1_periods, aes(x = state, y = events, fill = state)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = scales::comma(events)), vjust = -0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ period, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Arizona" = "#D55E00",
                               "California" = "#0072B2")) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
  labs(title = "Heat-event records by period, CA vs AZ",
       x = NULL, y = "Number of event records") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11))

Q1 finding: California and Arizona recorded similar numbers of heat events over 2007–2025: 2,622 records in Arizona vs 2,414 in California, and 398 vs 366 episodes. The answer is the same whether I count records or episodes, since both states average about 6.6 records per episode. Year to year, both states record few events before 2017, then rise sharply. Arizona jumps abruptly (24 in 2017 to 294 in 2018), while California climbs more gradually, peaking at 405 in 2021. Changes this sudden likely reflect changes in reporting rather than weather (see Additional analysis). The 2025 drop in both states may mean that year’s records are incomplete. By period, California recorded more events through 2017, Arizona pulled ahead in 2018–2021, and the two were nearly equal in 2022–2025. Since the two states have similar event counts, event frequency can’t explain the large gap in heat deaths.

Q2. How different are heat-related deaths after accounting for the number of heat events?

First I look at the distribution of deaths per event (expected to be heavily zero-inflated), then compare totals and deaths per event.

Q2 summary by state 
# Summarize event counts, deaths, and mortality measures by state.
q2_summary <- heat |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    n_events = n(),
    n_episodes = n_distinct(episode_id),
    deaths_direct = sum(deaths_direct),
    deaths_indirect = sum(deaths_indirect),
    total_deaths = sum(deaths_total),
    events_with_death = sum(deaths_total > 0),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    deaths_per_event = total_deaths / n_events,
    deaths_per_episode = total_deaths / n_episodes,
    pct_events_with_death = events_with_death / n_events
  )

Q2 plot data 
# Reshape the summary and format labels for plotting.
q2_plot_data <- q2_summary |>
  select(state, n_events, total_deaths, deaths_per_event) |>
  pivot_longer(
    -state,
    names_to = "measure",
    values_to = "value"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    measure = factor(
      measure,
      levels = c(
        "n_events",
        "total_deaths",
        "deaths_per_event"
      ),
      labels = c(
        "Heat events recorded",
        "Total heat deaths",
        "Deaths per heat event"
      )
    ),
    label = if_else(
      measure == "Deaths per heat event",
      sprintf("%.2f", value),
      scales::comma(value, accuracy = 1)
    )
  )

# Exploring the distribution of deaths per event, zoomed to 0–20 as the tail is too long to show.
ggplot(heat, aes(x = deaths_total, fill = state)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ state) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Arizona" = "#D55E00",
                               "California" = "#0072B2")) +
  labs(
    title = "Deaths per heat-event record, CA vs AZ",
    x = "Deaths per event record",
    y = "Number of records"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

Findings: Most heat events in both states record no deaths, but the distributions differ sharply. Most of California’s events record zero deaths, while in Arizona a much larger share record at least one, and Arizona has a long right tail. The chart is zoomed to 0–20, and a few Arizona events record far more (up to 150 in a single event). Because deaths are this skewed, the average deaths per event can be pulled up by a few extreme events, so I also compare the share of events with at least one death. As shown in the summary table above, at least one death was recorded in 40.2% of Arizona’s heat-event records, compared with 3.0% of California’s.

# Comparing total deaths and deaths per event
ggplot(q2_plot_data, aes(x = state, y = value, fill = state)) +
  geom_col() +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), vjust = -0.5) +
  facet_wrap(~ measure, scales = "free_y") +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Arizona" = "#D55E00",
      "California" = "#0072B2"
    )
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Similar numbers of heat events, but Arizona records\nabout 20 times more deaths per event",
    subtitle = "Heat and Excessive Heat events in Arizona and California, 2007-2025",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    axis.text.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid = element_blank()
  )

Q2 Finding: The difference in reported heat-related deaths remains large after accounting for the number of reported heat-event records. The two states recorded a similar number of heat events (2,622 vs 2,414), yet Arizona recorded 2,729 heat deaths compared with California’s 124. After normalizing by event count, Arizona averages 1.04 deaths per heat event versus 0.05 in California, roughly 20 times higher.

Why it matters: The roughly 20-fold difference in deaths per reported heat event shows that similar event counts can mask substantial differences in recorded loss of life. The gap remains large after adjusting for record counts, motivating me to examine whether direct or indirect deaths contribute more to the difference in Question 3.

Q3. Are mortality differences driven more by direct or indirect deaths?

Stacked bars show total burden (bar height) and composition (direct vs. indirect) per state; a proportional version isolates composition.

Q3 stacked deaths 
# Summarize direct and indirect deaths by state once; the Q3 cells below reuse this summary.
q3_summary <- heat |>
  group_by(state) |>
  summarise(
    Direct = sum(deaths_direct),
    Indirect = sum(deaths_indirect),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

q3 <- q3_summary |>
  pivot_longer(
    -state,
    names_to = "death_type",
    values_to = "deaths"
  )

print(q3)

q3_composition <- q3_summary |>
  mutate(
    Total = Direct + Indirect,
    Direct_share = Direct / Total,
    Indirect_share = Indirect / Total

To sum up, Arizona reported substantially more heat-related deaths than California from 2007-2025. The difference is primarily accounted for by direct deaths, which contribute about two-thirds of the gap between the states. However, the composition of mortality also differs: indirect deaths account for 32.5% of reported heat-related deaths in Arizona, compared with 16.1% in California. These differences reflect reported NOAA records and may also reflect differences in reporting practices across states.

Q4. Do CA and AZ differ in when heat deaths occur and how they have changed over time?

A month × year heatmap per state shows seasonality and trend together; an annual line chart compares long-term trends.

heat_monthly <- heat |>
  group_by(state, year, month) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths_total, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  complete(state, year = 2007:2025, month, fill = list(deaths = 0))
ggplot(heat_monthly, aes(x = year, y = month, fill = deaths)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.3) +
  facet_wrap(~ state, ncol = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "inferno", direction = -1,
                       trans = "log1p",
                       breaks = c(0, 1, 5, 20, 50, 100, 300)) +
  scale_y_discrete(limits = rev) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2007, 2025, 2), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(title = "Heat-related deaths by month and year",
       subtitle = "Color scale is log-transformed",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Deaths") +
  theme_minimal()

heat_monthly |>
  group_by(state, month) |>
  summarise(deaths = sum(deaths), .groups = "drop") |>
  group_by(state) |>
  mutate(share = round(100 * deaths / sum(deaths), 1)) |>
  arrange(state, desc(deaths))

Q4 finding:

Seasonality. In both states, heat deaths are concentrated in summer, but the timing differs. Arizona’s deaths are heavily concentrated in mid-summer: July alone accounts for 47.8% of all recorded heat deaths in 2007–2025, and June–August together account for 88.1%. California’s deaths are spread more evenly across a longer and later season. September is its peak month (31.5%), followed closely by July (29.8%) and June (21.0%), and June–September together account for 96.0%. Neither state records any heat deaths from November through February.

Change over time. The two states diverge sharply after 2017. From 2007 to 2017, Arizona recorded only 39 heat deaths in total (about 3.5 per year), similar to or below California. Starting in 2018, Arizona’s recorded deaths jump to 248 and stay high, peaking at 760 in 2023. Over 2018–2025 the state averages about 336 deaths per year. The heatmap also shows Arizona’s death season widening after 2018, with deaths now regularly recorded from April through September and in some years into October. California shows no comparable trend: its annual deaths stay low throughout, with occasional spikes such as 2007 (26 deaths) and a smaller one in 2024, and no clear widening of the season.

Reporting vs. real change. The jump in Arizona’s deaths in 2018 coincides with a jump in recorded heat events, from 24 in 2017 to 294 in 2018. Because deaths and event records rise in the same year, much of Arizona’s apparent increase likely reflects a change in how heat events and deaths were reported (see Additional analysis: Reporting differences), rather than a 100-fold increase in actual heat mortality. Arizona’s declines in 2024–2025 should also be read with caution, as recent NOAA records may not yet be complete.

Summary. Arizona’s recorded heat deaths are concentrated in July and rose sharply after 2018, while California’s are spread across June–September, peak later in the summer, and show no clear long-term trend. However, the size of Arizona’s increase is closely tied to changes in reporting, so the comparison of trends between the two states should be interpreted carefully.

Additional analysis: Reporting differences

Deaths in this dataset are entered by local NWS offices, based on what local health agencies tell them. If the two states report deaths differently, part of the gap could come from reporting rather than from real differences in mortality. I use the event narratives to check this.

Heat narr 
-- Loading narratives for the heat events. Join to the events file only to filter: keep narratives for CA/AZ heat events
select n.event_id, n.event_narrative
from "storm_event_narratives_2007_2025.csv" n
join "storm_events_2007_2025.csv" e on n.event_id = e.event_id
where e.state in ('CALIFORNIA', 'ARIZONA')
  and e.event_type in ('Heat', 'Excessive Heat')
# Check the join, preview the data, and count matched and unmatched records.
heat_narr_joined <- heat |>
  left_join(heat_narr, by = "event_id")

print(nrow(heat_narr_joined) == nrow(heat))

Finding: Recorded heat activity changes abruptly, not gradually. California has no heat events recorded in 2010. In Arizona, recorded events jump from 24 in 2017 to 294 in 2018, and recorded deaths from 2 to 248. Changes this sudden are more likely to reflect changes in how events were recorded than changes in the weather.

Unfortunately, the Maricopa County Department of Health was unable to provide details such as age, gender or circumstances regarding the deaths.
APACHE JUNCTION/GOLD CANYON 1 Very strong high pressure aloft developed over the southern deserts of Arizona beginning on July 23rd and this continued through July 25th, resulting in excessive heat across the lower deserts. The hotter lower deserts reached or exceeded 115 degrees each day which tied and broke records during the 3 day period. Phoenix reached 116 degrees on both the 24th and 25th; both marks tied or broke daily records. Low temperatures remained in the upper 80s to low 90s each morning resulting in very dangerous conditions especially for those spending time outdoors during the heat of the day. The presence of excessive heat was confirmed via locally derived heat risk data. Unfortunately, the excessive heat led to a fatality; a man was found dead in the open desert at 1605MST on July 24th. He was located about 3 miles southeast of Apache Junction, near the intersection of Baseline and Goldfield Roads. Paramedics and the fire department believed that the man’s death was due to the excessive heat. An Excessive Heat Warning was in effect at the time of the fatality.

Phoenix Sky Harbor recorded several days with highs reaching 115 degrees and 116 degrees during this time. According to Maricopa County Department of Public Health, there were 40 heat-associated deaths (32 direct and 8 indirect) that occurred during this event. Unfortunately, the Maricopa County Department of Health was unable to provide details such as age, gender or circumstances regarding the deaths.

Unfortunately, the Maricopa County Department of Health was unable to provide details such as age, gender or circumstances regarding the deaths.

Maricopa County’s health department appears frequently in the 2018 narratives. Checking whether the start time of narratives citing Maricopa County’s health department is related to the rise in recorded deaths in 2018.

Finding: Narratives citing the Maricopa County Department of Public Health appear every year from 2018 to 2024 and never before. The jump in Arizona’s recorded deaths lines up exactly with this source appearing.

However, does this mean Maricopa County’s heat deaths were never recorded before 2018?

# Checking how Maricopa deaths were recorded before 2018
heat_narr_joined |>
  filter(year < 2018, deaths_total == 0,
         str_detect(event_narrative, "Maricopa"), str_detect(event_narrative, "death")) |>
  select(year, event_narrative)
year event_narrative
2007 Maricopa County officials reported 32 confirmed deaths as either heat related or heat caused. Twenty four were male and 8 were female.
2008 A strong high pressure system resulted in record highs across the deserts. Phoenix tied the record on June 21 when the temperature hit 115 degrees. The average June temperature in Phoenix was 93.2 degrees, making it the fifth hottest June on record. In Maricopa County alone, 6 heat-related or heat-caused deaths were attributed to the heat.
2008 Heat was blamed as a factor in 9 deaths in the month of July for Maricopa County. Temperatures in Phoenix were above normal for much of the month, with this month being tied for the 17th warmest on record. The average minimum temperature was the 10th warmest, and a record |warm minimum of 90 degrees was set on July 1st. The high temperature in Phoenix on the 1st was 110.
2010 Maricopa County reported 2 heat related deaths and 3 heat caused deaths in August. The hottest high temperature was on the 5th when it reached 112 degrees in Phoenix. However, the highest daily average temperature was 101 degrees on the 24th.
2010 Very hot weather continued from August into September. Temperatures peaked at 111 in Phoenix and 113 in Gila Bend on the 3rd. The excessive heat may have been a contributing factor in three heat-related deaths in September in Maricopa County.
2010 The heat wave from late June continued into July. The last 3 days of June saw high temperatures over 110 degrees in Phoenix, and lows in the 80s. The average daily temperature was 101F on the last day of June, and remained over 100 through July 2nd. For the first two days of July the high temperature was 114. Excessive heat continued in Phoenix through the middle of the month, when the average daily temperature was 104 degrees on the 15th and the 16th. In Maricopa County alone, there were 44 heat caused or heat related deaths from late May through the end of the month of July. Hospitals across the Valley treated many patients with varying symptoms.

Finding: Before 2018, Maricopa deaths were sometimes mentioned only in the text. Six records from 2007-2010 mention about 99 confirmed or possible heat-related deaths in Maricopa County in their narratives, yet report zero deaths in the numeric fields. Arizona’s pre-2018 deaths are therefore undercounted, and the 2018 jump may partly reflect a change in reporting.

# Consider the change in reporting, do a robustness check by comparing 2007–2017 with 2018–2025

heat |>
  mutate(period = if_else(year >= 2018, "2018-2025", "2007-2017")) |>  # 2018 = Maricopa County began reporting to NWS
  group_by(state, period) |>
  summarise(events = n(),
            deaths = sum(deaths_total),
            deaths_per_event = deaths / events,
            .groups = "drop")
state period events deaths deaths_per_event
Arizona 2007-2017 135 39 0.2888889
Arizona 2018-2025 2487 2690 1.0816244
California 2007-2017 347 67 0.1930836
California 2018-2025 2067 57 0.0275762

Finding: The gap persists when both states are compared over 2018-2025. Arizona records about 1.08 deaths per event versus 0.03 in California. The gap even looks larger than over the full period (1.04 vs 0.05). This is because after 2018, California recorded about six times as many heat events (347 to 2,067) while its deaths stayed flat (67 to 57), so its deaths per event fell from 0.19 to 0.03. Arizona’s events and deaths both rose sharply, reflecting Maricopa County’s reporting.

However, this only explains when and why Arizona’s recorded deaths rose, not why Arizona records far more deaths than California.

California recorded 2,067 heat events in 2018–2025, compared with 347 in 2007–2017, while recorded deaths totaled 57 and 67, respectively. Since narratives revealed Arizona’s undercounting, I read the narratives of California’s deadliest heat events to see whether they mention more deaths than recorded.

Finding: The three 2024 Santa Clara records add up to 16 recorded deaths, while the narrative mentions 28 deaths under investigation as heat-related. Not all 28 may be confirmed as heat deaths, but this suggests California’s recorded deaths are likely an undercount, so the true gap between the states may be smaller than the data show.

Overall Finding in Additional Analysis:

I found clear differences in how heat deaths are reported. In Arizona, recorded deaths rose sharply in 2018 when Maricopa County began supplying death counts, and earlier deaths were sometimes mentioned only in the narratives. In California, the narratives suggest deaths are still undercounted, as in Santa Clara County in 2024. The gap between the states persists even after 2018, so Arizona’s early undercounting does not explain it. However, because reporting is incomplete in both states, the comparison should be read as a gap in recorded heat deaths, not a precise measure of true mortality.

4. Conclusions

Key findings

  • Heat-event frequency: Arizona and California recorded similar numbers of heat-event records during 2007–2025: 2,622 and 2,414, respectively. However, their annual patterns differed, with Arizona’s recorded events rising abruptly in 2018.

  • Deaths per reported event: Arizona recorded 2,729 heat-related deaths, compared with 124 in California. After accounting for event counts, Arizona averaged 1.04 deaths per reported event versus 0.05 in California—about 20 times higher.

  • Direct versus indirect deaths: Direct deaths accounted for approximately two-thirds of the mortality gap between the states. However, indirect deaths represented a larger share of Arizona’s recorded deaths than California’s: 32.5% versus 16.1%.

  • Seasonality and trends: Arizona’s recorded deaths were concentrated in July, which accounted for 47.8% of its total, while California’s deaths were more evenly distributed across June–September, with September contributing the largest share at 31.5%. Arizona’s recorded deaths rose sharply after 2018, while California showed no clear long-term trend.

  • Reporting differences: Event narratives suggest undercounting in both states, and changes in how Maricopa County’s deaths were recorded may partly explain Arizona’s increase in 2018. The gap remains when comparing only 2018–2025, but it should be interpreted as a difference in recorded deaths rather than a precise measure of the true mortality gap.

Limitations

  • NOAA storm-event death counts depend on local NWS office reporting practices and likely undercount heat deaths relative to public health records (e.g., death certificates). State differences may partly reflect reporting differences between offices rather than true differences in mortality.
  • Heat events are logged per forecast zone; counts depend on whether I use records or episodes (see Data Preparation), and zone definitions differ between states.
  • Heat vs. Excessive Heat classification follows office-specific warning criteria.
  • Only 3,480 of the 5,036 heat-event records could be matched to event narratives. My checks of reporting differences therefore cover only part of the dataset and may not capture all reporting issues.
  • Deaths per reported event do not account for differences in population size, heat intensity, event duration, or population vulnerability. They should therefore not be interpreted as a direct measure of residents’ mortality risk or as evidence of what causes the difference between the states.
